summary: Gather and adversarially verify evidence on Media Foundation vs DirectShow camera capture reliability on Windows

gaps: No long-run stability data on either API: the longest MF session is ~32 s, MJPEG cells are 10 s, bandwidth combos 3-6 s, PyAV DirectShow probes 6-10 s. Nothing local tests hour-long recordings, sleep/resume, or USB surprise-removal mid-stream on MF vs DirectShow.

No multi-process test: skellycam runs one OS process per camera, but every multi-camera MF and DirectShow test opened all cameras in one process (threads), and camlock serialized all other processes. MF/Frame Server behaviour with N capture processes is untested.
No test of two applications sharing one camera (Frame Server shared mode vs DirectShow exclusive access), and no test of a capture app coexisting with Teams/Zoom/LogiTune holding the camera.

Frame Server CPU and latency overhead are unmeasured (needs elevation). The 'MF adds 5-10 ms latency' claim in skellycam's determine_backend.py comment has no local measurement, for either OpenCV MSMF or raw MF.
DirectShow timestamps were never scored against the screen-flash ground truth; only MF (and libusb) timestamps were. The DirectShow comparison rests on PTS regularity and drift.
It was never tested whether the DirectShow (ksproxy) path really bypasses the Frame Server or skips UVC metadata; that rests on a comment in dshow_open_probe.cpp.
The cause of the ~94 s stall in the verifier's MF multi-open batch (va_stagger0_origexe) was not recorded: MF hang, hub-IOCTL topology snapshot, or harness stdout loop.

Why the generic camera re-enumerated (03:18:48Z, 04:12:37Z) after bandwidth refusals is unexplained. LastArrivalDate keeps only the latest arrival, so whether the 03:49Z DeviceNotFound was also a re-arrival cannot be told.

No local commit message or doc records why nokhwa (MF) was dropped for OpenCV DSHOW in 1388b7ae beyond 'trick was drop nokhwa for opencv'. The source of the user's 'MF is flaky' reports is not in the repo.

No external (web) reports were checked in this sweep; it was limited to local evidence. Known public OpenCV MSMF issues (slow open, buffering) are wrapper-level and should be kept apart from raw IMFSourceReader.
Kiyo-specific DirectShow vs MF differences (YUY2 fallback, 1080p60 MJPEG) were never re-tested because the Kiyo was excluded.
C930e exposure behaviour without LogiTuneAgent running is untested, so LogiTune resetting exposure cannot be ruled out as the cause of the -5 readback on all APIs.

verified.claim: Raw MF IMFSourceReader (native MJPG, converters disabled) delivered the camera's own JPEG at full rate, 100% valid, 0 gaps, on all three cameras, single and multi-camera, at 0.7-2.2% of one core.
verified.corrected_claim: Raw MF IMFSourceReader with native MJPG and MF_READWRITE_DISABLE_CONVERTERS kept MJPG as the output subtype. It delivered C922 30.00, C930e 30.05 and generic 25.76-25.78 fps (300/301/257-258 frames per 10 s, 0 gaps over 1.5 periods), 100% valid under the lenient decode, at 0.7-2.1% of one core for the capture process (Frame Server excluded). Every streaming test window was 10 s. The generic camera's 1080p frames fail strict libjpeg-turbo decoding on every frame, on MF and PyAV alike. In the 3-camera cells one shared-hub camera was refused bandwidth.
verified.note: Numbers match RESULTS.md and the summary.json fps I re-aggregated. The table's max is 2.1%, not 2.2%. The windows are short: this shows correctness, not long-run stability.

verified.claim: PyAV/FFmpeg DirectShow vcodec=mjpeg delivers byte-identical JPEG to MF at matching rates and similar CPU; on the data path the two are equivalent.
verified.corrected_claim: For each camera and mode, PyAV dshow vcodec=mjpeg (demux only) delivered JPEG whose full SOI..SOS header SHA-1 matches MF's. That is the camera's own encoder output, not a re-encode. Rates match MF: C922 30.0, C930e 30.04-30.05, generic 25.74. Process CPU was 0.9-1.6% for one camera and 2.7% (720p) / 3.0-3.1% (1080p) with two cameras streaming, against MF's 1.7% / 2.0% whole-process. On this machine the frame-data path is equivalent.
verified.note: Only the headers were compared; scan data naturally differs frame to frame. MF's CPU figure excludes Frame Server, so the CPU comparison is not like-for-like (see the Frame Server claim).

verified.claim: 71 mf_uvc_timing sessions (50,894 frames) had ReadSample errors only in 4 sessions, all on the faulted Razer Kiyo.
verified.corrected_claim: Across 106 *.session.json files under results/windows/Gerald (50,894 frames total), only 4 sessions had errors: all are the Razer Kiyo, 21 errors and 0 frames each (flash_run1_repositioned, kiyo_check, meta_check1, verify_rerun_vflash1). These sessions are short (tens of seconds). They come from mf_uvc_timing only, so they leave out the MF failures seen elsewhere (MF_E_REBOOT_REQUIRED, bandwidth refusals, DeviceNotFound).
verified.note: The frame total and error pattern match, but I count 106 session files, not 71; the report may have de-duplicated copies, and the method is not stated. The scope is a single tool, and nothing ran longer than about 32 s.

verified.claim: The overnight rerun saw only expected bandwidth refusals on both APIs plus two transient MF DeviceNotFound misses; no MF_E_REBOOT_REQUIRED, no 0x8007001F.
verified.corrected_claim: In the 10-27/28 unattended rerun (Kiyo excluded, no device restarts), the only failures were shared-hub bandwidth refusals (MF 0x800718CF, DirectShow OSError 5) and two transient MF DeviceNotFound misses of the generic camera, each straight after a refusal. There was no MF_E_REBOOT_REQUIRED and no 0x8007001F. One verifier batch of MF multi-open also stalled for about 94 s and was killed.
verified.note: The text matches. The same document (line ~46) also records the hung run_concurrency combo killed after about 94 s, which belongs in any 'failures seen' summary.

verified.claim: After vetoed pnputil restarts left DN_NEED_RESTART on camera interface devnodes, every MF open failed with MF_E_REBOOT_REQUIRED while PyAV DirectShow still captured 192 MJPEG frames from the C922.
verified.corrected_claim: On 2026-10-25, MetadataBufferSizeInKB0=5 was written at 14:09:33 local to enable MF's UVC metadata. The follow-up pnputil /restart-device then returned 3010 ('System reboot is needed'), with LogiTuneAgent vetoing removal (Kernel-PnP 225). That left DN_NEED_RESTART (0x0180610A) on the camera MI_00 devnodes. Meanwhile mf_multi_open failed at ActivateObject with 0xC00D7167 MF_E_REBOOT_REQUIRED for the C922, Kiyo and C930e, and nokhwa MF failed the same way. PyAV DirectShow still captured 192 valid MJPEG frames from the C922 at 14:11:50 local. A replug cleared it.
verified.note: Confirmed. The missing context is that the trigger was the registry change needed to enable MF's own UVC-metadata feature, followed by a vetoed device restart. It is self-inflicted setup, not spontaneous MF flakiness, and it would recur when that metadata registry value is enabled on a user machine running LogiTune. Only one DirectShow cell (C922) ran in the window.

verified.claim: DN_NEED_RESTART on only the usbccgp composite parent does not block MF; only the flag on the MI_00 devnode does.
verified.corrected_claim: In one recheck at 14:41 local on 10-25, the C922 and C930e captured through MF (113 and 108 frames) while their usbccgp parents still showed 0x0180610A (DN_NEED_RESTART) and their MI_00 interfaces were clear (0x0180600A). That one observation suggests only the interface flag blocks MF.
verified.note: A single observation on two cameras. The same file corrects an earlier mislabelling in devnode_status_1439.json.

verified.claim: The Kiyo Pro EP0 firmware fault breaks every API equally; when healthy, MF and PyAV DirectShow both streamed it.
verified.corrected_claim: From 15:03 to 15:22 local on 10-25, the Kiyo Pro failed on KS-direct (CT GET ERROR_GEN_FAILURE in ~7 ms), raw MF (0x8007001F at first ReadSample, 10/10 modes), OpenCV MSMF (opens, grab fails), OpenCV DSHOW (open fails), PyAV dshow ('Could not RenderStream') and a minimal DirectShow graph (IAMCameraControl::Get 0x8007001F, RenderStream 0x80070057). Hub-IOCTL string-descriptor reads also failed. After replugs it streamed on PyAV dshow (362 frames, 14:17), SDL3 MF (151, 14:19), the MF reader (335, 14:49) and mfvideosrc (155, 14:51).
verified.note: Confirmed by the timeline. mjpeg_mf_recheck/summary.json says the Kiyo 'recovered without a replug', which contradicts the timeline's second replug at 14:48. Every observed fault onset came after the metadata registry change (see the MetadataBufferSizeInKB0 claim).

verified.claim: On MF a fault surfaces at the first ReadSample; on DirectShow at graph build/open; OpenCV MSMF reports isOpened()=true then fails at first grab.
verified.corrected_claim: For bandwidth refusals and the Kiyo fault, MF activate, source reader and SetCurrentMediaType all succeeded (setup 26-71 ms), and the error appeared at the first ReadSample (0x800718CF or 0x8007001F). DirectShow paths failed at open or graph build (PyAV OSError 5 or RenderStream; OpenCV DSHOW 'open failed'). OpenCV MSMF opened and then failed at grab. A health check on MF therefore has to read at least one sample.
verified.note: Matches the files.

verified.claim: MF's bandwidth refusal is specific (0x800718CF, Win32 6351) while FFmpeg DirectShow gives only OSError(5) and OpenCV DSHOW only 'open failed'.
verified.corrected_claim: MF returned the self-describing 0x800718CF ('A camera interface doesn't have the desired bandwidth for data transfer'). Through PyAV, the DirectShow refusal reached Python only as OSError(5, 'I/O error'), and OpenCV DSHOW as 'open failed'. FFmpeg's dshow log can carry more detail: the Kiyo fault showed 'Could not RenderStream to connect pins'. So the generic text partly reflects how the harness captured logs, and a custom DirectShow graph would see the RenderStream HRESULT.
verified.note: The MF side holds. The claim about DirectShow's error detail is limited to the wrapper (PyAV/OpenCV), not the DirectShow API.

verified.claim: Bandwidth admission is the same on both APIs; the C930e and generic cannot both stream on the shared hub; neither API offers bandwidth control.
verified.corrected_claim: usbvideo picks the same alt per camera and mode (32/32), and the C930e and generic camera on one Genesys USB 2.0 hub could not both stream MJPG at 720p or 1080p on MF, PyAV dshow or OpenCV DSHOW. An 80% budget model predicted 26/26 outcomes. No surveyed library controls bandwidth through MF, DirectShow, KS or AVFoundation.
verified.note: The 'no control' part is inferred from a survey of docs and source.

verified.claim: MF without stagger: the loser is a start race; with a 2.5 s stagger the second-started camera loses; DirectShow opened sequentially and the last-opened lost.
verified.corrected_claim: With MF and stagger 0, a different camera lost in 3 of 4 over-budget combos (confirmed with the original binary). With a 2.5 s stagger, the second-started camera always got 0x800718CF. In the two PyAV/OpenCV DirectShow 3-camera cells (sequential open), the generic camera opened last and failed to open. With nokhwa (MF) the generic lost 3/3, start order unrecorded.
verified.source: RERUN_20261027.md goal 3 and libusb tables; mjpeg/RESULTS.md:109; bw_adversarial_verify_20261028/va_stagger0_origexe.json
verified.note: The DirectShow evidence is only a handful of cells in fixed open order, so DirectShow non-determinism was never tested.

verified.claim: Twice after a refusal MF briefly could not find the generic camera; one lines up to the millisecond with a USB re-arrival; the other re-arrival happened in an OpenCV DSHOW cell; so it is hub/camera behaviour, not an MF fault.
verified.corrected_claim: r07 combo c930e_alt10_then_gen ended at 03:18:48.175Z with the generic camera refused (0x800718CF). The next MF combo got DeviceNotFound, and the generic devnode's LastArrivalDate is 03:18:48.328-.342Z, about 150 ms after the MF processes closed, so the camera re-enumerated right as MF released it. A second re-arrival (04:12:37Z) fell inside an OpenCV DSHOW 3-camera cell (started 04:12:20Z) where the generic camera was refused. Both re-enumerations followed refused opens, one on each API, which points to camera or hub behaviour, but the cause is unproven.
verified.note: 'Up to the millisecond' is wrong: the gap is about 150 ms. The 04:12:37Z time appears only in the md text; I found no JSON record of it. The second DeviceNotFound (verifier, 03:49Z) has no arrival record.

verified.claim: One MF multi-open verifier batch stalled about 94 s on its 6th combo and was killed; cause not recorded; harness stdout loop has no timeout.
verified.corrected_claim: In the verifier's MF multi-open batch (original 10-25 binary, stagger 0, C930e + generic), 5 of 8 combos completed (with 0x800718CF refusals and one DeviceNotFound). The 6th (gen_then_c930e720_2) was still running about 94 s after combo 5 ended at 03:50:12Z and was killed by the outer 200 s camlock timeout. The cause is unknown: an MF hang (synchronous ReadSample has no timeout), the hub-IOCTL snapshot subprocess (60 s timeout), or the untimed `for line in p.stdout` loop. No process was left behind and the devnodes were OK.
verified.note: The facts are confirmed. 'Favours DS' is not supported: there was no comparable DirectShow stress batch, and the cause may lie in the harness.

verified.claim: Raw MF opens fast (setup 26-92 ms, first sample 57-960 ms later); PyAV DirectShow open 385-812 ms.
verified.corrected_claim: For MF, ActivateObject + reader + SetCurrentMediaType took 25.7-92.3 ms (medians C922 31.5, C930e 41.4, generic 28.0 ms), and the first sample came 57-960 ms after that (medians 302/474/76 ms). PyAV dshow open (graph build and start) took 385-812 ms, with time to first packet not separately reported. Measured as time to first frame, the two are of the same order on the Logitech cameras (MF roughly 270-1050 ms).
verified.note: Numbers reproduced exactly. 'MF opens fast' compares MF setup alone against a DirectShow figure that includes starting the stream, so the comparison is not like-for-like.

verified.claim: OpenCV CAP_MSMF opens Logitech cameras in 39-41 s (45 s on 5.0.0) and the generic in 3.4-3.7 s; raw MF opens in ~30-90 ms, so the delay is the wrapper (hypothesis: walking ~335 native types).
verified.corrected_claim: OpenCV 4.12 CAP_MSMF open_ms was about 39-41 s for the C922/C930e and 3.35-3.69 s for the generic camera; raw MF setup on the same cameras was 26-92 ms. So the delay is in OpenCV's MSMF wrapper, not in MF. The cause is unmeasured. OpenCV documents OPENCV_VIDEOIO_MSMF_ENABLE_HW_TRANSFORMS=0 as possibly shortening init, and that was not tested.
verified.source: mjpeg/RESULTS.md:128-135,361-362; re-aggregated mjpeg_opencv-msmf-*/summary.json (3354-40358 ms valid cells)
verified.note: An external report (OpenCV forum, 2024-10-14) shows the same ~40 s MSMF init plus ~39 s per property set on a capture card, with DSHOW instant. That matches a wrapper problem and is a likely source of 'MF is flaky/slow' folklore.

verified.claim: The earlier 'MSMF gives 0 frames' was a harness bug (30 s open wait vs ~40 s open), not an MF failure.
verified.corrected_claim: The 10-25 OpenCV MSMF '0 frames, ~93% CPU' result was a harness artifact: the script waited 30 s for a 39-41 s open. With --open-wait 90 it ran at 30 fps (46-54% CPU decoding). This is an OpenCV MSMF wrapper result, not raw MF.
verified.note: Confirmed, including by the verifier.

verified.claim: OpenCV CAP_MSMF wrapper quirks: never returns JPEG, pads the 25.7 fps generic to 30 fps with duplicates, raw NV12 ran 17.1 fps; raw MF gave a true 25.76 fps.
verified.corrected_claim: OpenCV 4.12 CAP_MSMF returned decoded BGR (46-54% of one core at 720p, 143-156% at 1080p) or MF-decoded NV12 as a 1-row Mat, never JPEG. On the generic camera it reported about 30 fps with about 48 of 300 frames pixel-identical to the previous one (unique rate 25.3-25.4 fps; the verifier found 47/300). Its raw NV12 mode ran that camera at 17.13 fps. Raw MF and OpenCV DSHOW ran it at 25.7-25.8 fps with no repeats.
verified.note: These are wrapper defects, not raw-MF defects.

verified.claim: OpenCV CAP_DSHOW wrapper quirks: never JPEG, property-order dependence (fourcc-first YUY2 9.99 fps vs size-first MJPG 30 fps), opens 1.4-4.0 s.
verified.corrected_claim: OpenCV 4.12 CAP_DSHOW returned BGR only (24.6-28.3% of one core at 720p, 37-40% at 1080p, still BGR with CONVERT_RGB=0). Setting FOURCC first negotiated YUY2 at 9.99 fps; setting size first negotiated MJPG at 30 fps. Opens took 1418-4013 ms.
verified.source: mjpeg/RESULTS.md:122-127; RERUN_20261027.md goal 1 table; re-aggregated mjpeg_opencv-dshow-*/summary.json
verified.note: Numbers reproduced.

verified.claim: The skellycam team hit the same DSHOW order-of-operations quirk; nokhwa (MF) was dropped for OpenCV DSHOW without a recorded reason.
verified.corrected_claim: Commit 1388b7ae (jonmatthis, 2026-05-11, upstream/development-try-tauri) says 'trick was drop nokhwa for opencv and getting DSHOW and MJPG to work ... key is to set stuff after initial frame read', and thread.rs adds 'FOURCC must be set AGAIN after the first read()'. nokhwa was used with features=['input-native'] (MSMF on Windows). Neither that commit nor the plan update a4a5eeb0 ('swap nokhwa for opencv') records why nokhwa was dropped.
verified.source: git show 1388b7ae; git show a4a5eeb0; git show 5fce5d7d:skellycam-rust/skellycam/Cargo.toml
verified.note: Confirmed. It is plausible but unproven that nokhwa's format-list bug (hiding MJPEG on the Logitech cameras) was the trigger.

verified.claim: nokhwa's MF backend has wrapper bugs (format list hides MJPEG on Logitech, fails on NDI virtual cameras); exact MJPEG requests still stream natively.
verified.corrected_claim: nokhwa 0.10.11's format list keeps at most 2 FourCCs and so hides MJPEG on the Logitech cameras. An exact MJPEG request still streamed natively (593/593, 588/588, 515/515 valid frames). Listing failed on the NDI virtual cameras with 'Failed to fulfill requested format'.
verified.note: These are wrapper bugs, which can look like 'MF flakiness' to an application developer.

verified.claim: skellycam chose CAP_DSHOW citing MSMF decode-transform latency 5-10 ms and ignored BUFFERSIZE; no local measurement backs it and raw MF with converters disabled has no decode transform.
verified.corrected_claim: On the development branch, determine_backend.py states that MSMF 'adds a decode transform pipeline with internal buffering that increases latency by 5-10ms' and ignores CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE, and create_cv2_video_capture.py says MSMF ignores BUFFERSIZE while DSHOW respects it. These are uncited comments about OpenCV's wrappers. With MF_READWRITE_DISABLE_CONVERTERS, raw MF keeps MJPG output and has no decoder MFT in the reader.
verified.note: The quotes match. The 5-10 ms claim is unmeasured anywhere in the repo. 'Favours DS' applies only to OpenCV MSMF against OpenCV DSHOW.

verified.claim: Timestamp quality favours MF: MF sample time equals the device timestamp and scored 4.40-4.52 ms; MF carries UVC PTS (~0.5 ms); DirectShow sample time is synthesized and drifts.
verified.corrected_claim: MF's sample time (= device timestamp) sits on the same ~16 ms grid as host arrival and scored 4.40-4.52 ms on the C922, against 4.59-4.98 ms for arrival. That is essentially no better. FFmpeg dshow's graph-clock mode (use_video_device_timestamps=0) also follows arrival on the same grid. The real MF advantage is the UVC PTS/SCR in capture metadata: 0.47-0.68 ms on the C922, which is the method's floor. The C930e's PTS is synthetic and mode-dependent, and the generic camera has none. DirectShow's default device sample time is constant-interval: +141 ms/s drift on the generic camera, about -1.5 to -1.8 ms/s on the C930e.
verified.source: REPORT.md:32-34,110-114; prior_art/SURVEY.md:50,56-70; RERUN_20261027.md goal 2 and prior-art tables
verified.note: The advantage is real only with UVC metadata, and only on cameras with a real PTS (here, the C922). DirectShow timestamps were never scored against the flash ground truth.

verified.claim: Host arrival time is quantized to ~16 ms on every Windows path (MF, KS, FFmpeg dshow graph clock); the quantization sits below MF.
verified.corrected_claim: Every arrival-tracking timestamp (mfvideosrc, ksvideosrc, SDL3 MF sample time, FFmpeg dshow graph-clock mode) falls on ~16 ms multiples. It appears on the KS path as well, so it originates below MF (usbvideo or the USB stack). timeBeginPeriod(1) reduces arrival-phase jitter but not the quantization.
verified.note: The mechanism (isochronous completion boundaries) is an unverified hypothesis.

verified.claim: UVC PTS/SCR metadata is available only through MF once MetadataBufferSizeInKB0 is set; it did not change frame delivery; DirectShow never requests it (untested).
verified.corrected_claim: With MetadataBufferSizeInKB0 set (admin, per camera interface, then a device restart or replug), MF samples carried the UVC payload header on the C922 and C930e (353/353 and 348/348 frames), and frame delivery was unchanged. The generic camera, without the value set, had none. Whether DirectShow, ksproxy or KS-direct clients can get it was not tested; 'DirectShow never requests it' is a code comment.
verified.source: mjpeg/RESULTS.md:141-144; timing/src/dshow_open_probe.cpp:1-2; PROGRESS.md (UVC metadata registry row)
verified.note: 'Only through MF' is not shown. Enabling the value requires a device restart, which LogiTune vetoed on this machine and which caused the MF_E_REBOOT_REQUIRED incident.

verified.claim: C930e manual exposure not applied is camera/driver behaviour: reads -7 after set, -5 after streaming on every API.
verified.corrected_claim: In all 26 C930e cells (raw MF, MF-decoded, PyAV dshow, OpenCV DSHOW decode/raw, OpenCV MSMF decode/raw, WinRT), exposure read -5 before the set, -7 right after the set and at the end of the apply step, and -5 again on the post-capture readback. In MF flash runs only 1 of 4 valid -7 runs integrated about 2^-7 s. LogiTuneAgent was running throughout (it respawns), so LogiTune resetting the control cannot be excluded.
verified.note: In the MJPEG matrix, controls were applied with mf_mjpeg_capture --controls-only --via-dshow, so even the MF cells set controls through the DirectShow path.

verified.claim: Camera controls work from MF: the MF device source exposes the same KS-proxy IAMCameraControl/IAMVideoProcAmp, so no DirectShow graph is needed.
verified.corrected_claim: mf_uvc_timing.cpp QueryInterfaces IAMCameraControl and IAMVideoProcAmp on the IMFMediaSource and sets exposure and white balance there. On the C922 the exposure readback matched the request (-7/-9/-6) and the flash results agree. On the C930e the same MF path read back the requested value but did not apply it in 3 of 4 runs. The MJPEG matrix applied controls via DirectShow (--via-dshow), not MF.
verified.note: The API route works. A readback matching the request does not prove the setting took effect.

verified.claim: WinRT MediaFrameReader cannot deliver MJPG (E_INVALIDARG) and sometimes got no callbacks; a WinRT-layer limitation.
verified.corrected_claim: WinRT MediaFrameReader with outputSubtype MJPG raised 0x80070057 on every TryAcquireLatestFrame (all three cameras, all variants). There were no FrameArrived callbacks at all for the C930e 720p single-camera cell or for the generic camera in both all-three cells. With no subtype it delivered NV12. Raw IMFSourceReader on the same cameras delivered MJPG.
verified.note: This reinforces that 'MF route' results depend heavily on the layer used.

verified.claim: Frame Server CPU could not be measured unelevated; the MF-vs-DS CPU comparison is biased toward MF by an unknown amount.
verified.corrected_claim: Frame Server CPU could not be read without elevation (OpenProcess error 5; frameserver_cpu_pct_of_one_core null), so the MF, WinRT and OpenCV-MSMF CPU figures exclude it. The DirectShow (ksproxy) figures are assumed to have no such hidden cost, which is also unverified.
verified.note: Confirmed.

verified.claim: DirectShow lists software-only virtual cameras MF does not (OBS, NVIDIA Broadcast, SpoutCam); MF 8 vs DS 15; indices unstable on both.
verified.corrected_claim: On this machine MF lists 8 sources (4 NDI plus 4 USB) and DirectShow lists 15 (the same plus OBS-Camera 1-4, OBS Virtual Camera, Camera (NVIDIA Broadcast) and SpoutCam, with no device path). Indices changed across devnode re-creation on both APIs. This cuts both ways: MF filters out junk devices, but it cannot open DirectShow-only virtual cameras that a user might want to use.
verified.note: Chromium's factory code also states 'DirectShow virtual cameras are not supported by MediaFoundation' and adds them from DirectShow. That makes this a con for MF if virtual cameras matter, rather than a pure MF win.

verified.claim: Both APIs can open by stable device path without touching other cameras; MFEnumDeviceSources activates nothing; enumerate-and-activate is a library problem.
verified.corrected_claim: MF opening by symbolic link (filtered activation) and FFmpeg dshow opening by alternative name both touched only the listed cameras. mf_mjpeg_capture --list-enum calls only MFEnumDeviceSources, with no activation. SDL3 (MF), openpnp-capture (DirectShow), GStreamer ksvideosrc and libusb enumeration touch every camera, which is a library choice.
verified.note: Matches the code and the document.

verified.claim: FFmpeg DirectShow can silently deliver a different format (Kiyo came back as rawvideo YUY2 with vcodec=mjpeg); MF's tool verifies the output subtype.
verified.corrected_claim: Once, at 18:13Z on 10-25 (inside the DN_NEED_RESTART/MF_E_REBOOT_REQUIRED window), PyAV dshow with vcodec=mjpeg opened the Kiyo Pro as codec rawvideo (YUY2, 1,843,200-byte packets). It was never reproduced. This was not silent: PyAV reports the stream codec, so it is detectable. The MF tool's subtype check is a harness feature.
verified.note: A single anomalous run on an excluded, faulty device while the device was in a bad state, so it is weak evidence against DirectShow.

verified.claim: Multi-camera in one process works on both APIs when bandwidth allows; MF C930e 30.05 vs PyAV 29.85 in 3-camera 1080p.
verified.corrected_claim: In the single-process 3-camera cells, MF streamed the C922 at 30.00 and the C930e at 30.05 fps at 1080p, and PyAV dshow streamed them at 30.00 and 29.85 fps. The generic camera was refused on both. nokhwa (MF) also streamed the C922 + C930e concurrently. Multi-process capture (skellycam's model) was never tested on either API.
verified.source: mjpeg/RESULTS.md matrix rows 205-206, 217-218; RERUN_20261027.md libusb table
verified.note: Each was a single 10 s cell.

verified.claim: Other MF consumers were reliable: mfvideosrc 172/172, 167/167, 154/154; SDL3 4/4 incl. Kiyo when healthy; nokhwa native MJPEG.
verified.corrected_claim: GStreamer 1.28 mfvideosrc (rerun 172/172, 167/167, 154/154; earlier 172/155/168), SDL3 3.4.18 on MF (170/153/151/167 on 4 cameras including the Kiyo, all valid) and nokhwa 0.10.11 MSMF (593/588/515) all delivered native MJPEG in short runs.
verified.source: prior_art/SURVEY.md:48,53; RERUN_20261027.md prior-art and libusb tables
verified.note: Runs of a few seconds each, so this does not test long-run stability.

verified.claim: MF cannot be told to skip capture metadata; enabling it was ruled out as the Kiyo fault cause because KS-direct also fails.
verified.corrected_claim: The probe's comment says MetadataBufferSizeInKB0 is the only switch for MF capture metadata. The Kiyo fault also hit KS-direct control GETs and hub-IOCTL string-descriptor reads, which do not use the streaming pin. That points to a device or EP0 fault. ClockRes showed max 15.600 ms, min 0.500 ms, current 1.000 ms on his Win7 SP1 machine. Another comment names multimedia timers as a common cause of the higher rate. A later commenter links a utility (lucashale.com) that changes the system timer. The post does not mention C#/P/Invoke code to fix it, NtSetTimerResolution or the registry. 'During system initialization, Windows checks if the TSC is suitable.' The FAQ says no validation is needed, thread affinity is 'neither necessary nor desirable', and QPC 'does not go backward'. QPC values from different threads have a ±1 tick ordering ambiguity.

The XP-era 'Performance counter value may unexpectedly leap forward' bug (Microsoft KB274323) made QueryPerformanceCounter jump on certain chipsets, and real projects shipped code workarounds (pjproject, PortAudio ticket, Mozilla leap-detection heuristic). This is a genuine Windows timer bug that needed application code, unlike the timer-resolution design behaviour. It is XP/2003-era and superseded by the Vista+ QPC design. A one-time perf_counter->UTC anchor therefore drifts from NTP-corrected wall time over long recordings, which matters if skellycam UTC timestamps are compared with other machines or devices. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/acquiring-high-resolution-time-stamps

I did not measure DirectShow device timestamps directly, that is, IMediaSample::GetTime on a capture pin with a running graph clock. Local evidence covers only the PyAV dshow pts drift, so whether a custom DirectShow capture-pin graph gives timestamps as good as MF llTimestamp is still open.
Chromium's MF blocklist names specific devices (LifeCam Studio, HP HD Camera, and others) but I did not open the linked crbug entries to read the failure modes or the Windows versions involved.

verified.claim: Microsoft Learn labels DirectShow a legacy feature superseded by MF capture, strongly recommends new code use MF capture and existing code be rewritten; same banner on Smart Tee, Time Stamps and MJPEG Decompressor pages.
verified.corrected_claim: Microsoft Learn's DirectShow pages, including Smart Tee, Time Stamps and MJPEG Decompressor, carry a banner. It calls DirectShow a legacy feature superseded by MediaPlayer, IMFMediaEngine and Audio/Video Capture in Media Foundation, strongly recommends that new code use those, and suggests rewriting existing code 'if possible'. No removal date is given.
verified.note: The quote matches word for word. It is a generic banner, not a capture-specific finding, and states no deprecation timeline.

verified.claim: Microsoft driver docs call the DirectShow capture pipeline 'in maintenance mode', lagging behind the MF pipeline that gets new OS features.
verified.corrected_claim: Microsoft's DShow Bridge guidance for UVC devices says: 'The modern pipeline is more thoroughly documented and utilizes the features added to the OS over the multiple releases. The legacy pipeline, being in maintenance mode, lags behind.'
verified.note: The quote is exact. It appears in the bullet that explains why a device might opt in or out of the bridge.

verified.claim: DShow Bridge routes DirectShow capture through MF/Frame Server, but each UVC device must opt in with EnableDshowRedirection bit 0x1; only then can a DS app share the camera.
verified.corrected_claim: A UVC device can opt into DShow Bridge on Windows 10 1607 and later. It does so through a Microsoft OS descriptor that creates EnableDshowRedirection (bit 0x1) under Enum\USB\<VID&PID>\<Instance>\Device Parameters. With the opt-in, DShow apps and sharing apps can use the camera concurrently. The opt-in is not the only route: the UVC implementation guide says devices that publish UVC-CPV2FaceAuth do not need EnableDshowRedirection.
verified.note: The quotes and the registry layout are accurate. 'Each device must opt in with this value' is too absolute: FaceAuth devices are bridged without it. In 1607 itself, DS apps were evidently routed through Frame Server without any opt-in (see the 1607 claim).

verified.claim: Bit 0x2 makes Frame Server decode MJPEG once and offer YUY2; bridged DS apps on such a camera would see no MJPEG.
verified.corrected_claim: Bit 0x2 of EnableDshowRedirection enables MJPEG decoding once in Frame Server and exposes the translated uncompressed (YUY2) types to multiple applications. The doc's value table implies MJPEG is then not exposed. This is a Frame Server setting, so it would affect MF/Frame Server clients as well as bridged DS apps.
verified.note: Framing it as a DS-only effect is misleading. The doc says the translated formats are 'offered to the multiple applications' served by Frame Server, which includes MF apps. That makes it an MJPEG risk for the MF path too, not only for bridged DS.

verified.claim: On the test machine none of the cameras is opted into DShow Bridge and each DS filter is the classic KS proxy, so DS capture most likely bypasses Frame Server.
verified.corrected_claim: I re-read the registry read-only. EnableDshowRedirection, UVC-CPV2FaceAuth and EnableFrameServerMode are absent for the C922, both C930e instances, 4C4A:4A55 and all three Kiyo instances, and each interface has a CLSID value (KS proxy). HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\OEM\DshowBridge (and its WOW6432Node copy) does exist, with one entry: Application=Launcher_Main.exe, Productname=Logitech Camera Software. Bridging therefore also appears to be decided per application. That DS capture of these cameras bypasses Frame Server is a plausible inference, not a measurement.
verified.note: The registry facts reproduce. The report missed the application-keyed OEM DshowBridge list, which shows the routing decision is not purely per camera. The bypass is inferred, not observed (no process or handle trace was taken).

verified.claim: mfksproxy.dll ('Dshow MF Bridge DLL') provides a DS filter backed by MF sensor groups; bridging is decided per camera via MFIsCameraDShowBridged and SOFTWARE\Microsoft\OEM\DshowBridge.
verified.corrected_claim: mfksproxy.dll (FileDescription 'Dshow MF Bridge DLL DLL', 10.0.26100.9549) is present, and CLSID {95FEE196-49F0-4C30-B16C-22C7B75C18EC} is registered as 'Dshow Camera MF Filter'. The DLL references SOFTWARE\Microsoft\OEM\DshowBridge and the value names 'Application' and 'ProductName'. On this machine that key lists an application (Logitech Camera Software, Launcher_Main.exe), not a camera, so the key appears to be a per-application list.
verified.source: C:\Windows\System32\mfksproxy.dll strings and version; HKCR\CLSID; HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\OEM\DshowBridge (local)
verified.note: The DLL facts are confirmed. Calling it 'per camera' is wrong for the OEM key. Its exact semantics (include list or exclude list) are undocumented.

verified.claim: An HLK test requires camera drivers to opt into DShow Bridge, so certified (mostly integrated) cameras route DS through Frame Server and generic USB webcams do not.
verified.corrected_claim: The HLK test 'Camera Driver System Test - Camera validation for DShow Bridge enablement' says it 'validates that all camera drivers always opt into DShow enablement'. It sits under the System.Client.Camera.VideoCapture spec, is categorised 'Development', and lists Windows 10 1803, 1809, 1903 and 'Next update'. Nothing on the page says how generic, uncertified USB webcams behave.
verified.note: The quote is accurate. It is a system (OEM) test in the Development category, so the conclusions about certified versus generic cameras are inference.

verified.claim: The Windows-Camera wiki says Frame Server sharing mode works for Win32 Capture Engine apps but not DirectShow apps.
verified.corrected_claim: The Microsoft Windows-Camera wiki FAQ says: 'sharing mode could also be used in Capture Engine (Win32) apps, but not in DirectShow apps.' For Capture Engine it is enabled through sensor groups (MFCreateSensorGroup), and the cleanest API is WinRT MediaCapture.
verified.note: The wiki is undated, so it may predate the Windows 11 'Allow multiple apps' toggle.

verified.claim: A Microsoft contributor called DirectShow legacy and no longer worked on; DS-filter virtual cameras are invisible to the Camera app and Settings and are capability-limited versus IMFVirtualCamera.
verified.corrected_claim: On 2024-11-19, LPBourret wrote in Windows-Camera issue #72 that 'DShow is considered legacy technology at this point (not worked on anymore nor encouraged to use v.s. newer MF APIs)'. The comment is about DShow-filter virtual cameras such as OBS's: they are not available in the Windows Camera app or the Settings page, have a limited capability set (no extended controls, single pin), and 'can incur issues if modified from 1 client while concurrently used from another'. The same comment says 'Some apps do still support DShow sources in some capacity such as Teams, Skype, Zoom.'
verified.note: The quote is exact (checked through the GitHub API). It concerns virtual cameras, not physical UVC capture reliability.

verified.claim: The Windows 11 'Allow multiple apps' toggle forces a single media type and requires Settings for basic controls, which matters for MJPEG mocap.
verified.corrected_claim: On 2026-02-05 LPBourret wrote that the multi-app camera feature is available on Windows 11 under Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Cameras > <camera> > Advanced camera options > 'Allow multiple apps..', and that it 'comes with some drawbacks however such as forcing a single MediaType, needing to use OS Settings page for basic camera controls, etc.' The comment does not say which media type is forced, or whether it affects MJPEG or non-bridged DS apps.
verified.note: The quote is exact. Its relevance to MJPEG mocap is the report's inference, and I did not re-check the Insider build 27758 detail. The feature is opt-in per camera, so it is not a default risk.

verified.claim: Microsoft documents that DS cannot use Sensor Groups, the mechanism behind Frame Server sharing, grouped RGB+IR and MF virtual cameras; IR/depth appear to DS as plain capture streams.
verified.corrected_claim: The UVC Camera Implementation Guide has a note, in the section on FSSensorGroupID/FSSensorGroupName INF entries, saying 'Sensor Groups are not supported in DShow capture pipeline.' It also says 'IR streams will show up as regular capture streams in DShow' and 'Depth streams show up as regular capture streams in DShow.'
verified.note: The three quotes are exact. Describing Sensor Groups as 'the mechanism behind Frame Server sharing ... and MF virtual-camera sources' is the report's own gloss, not what this doc says. The note is about multi-sensor grouping, which is irrelevant to single RGB UVC webcams.

verified.claim: MFCreateVirtualCamera (build 22000+) registers by default under the DS categories too; Frame Server custom media sources reach DS apps only if they also register them.
verified.corrected_claim: If categories is nullptr, MFCreateVirtualCamera registers under KSCATEGORY_VIDEO_CAMERA, KSCATEGORY_VIDEO and KSCATEGORY_CAPTURE (minimum client Windows Build 22000). The Frame Server Custom Media Source doc says: 'To allow enumeration by legacy DirectShow applications, your driver needs to also register under the KSCATEGORY_VIDEO and KSCATEGORY_CAPTURE.' It also recommends exposing YUY2, because legacy DS apps assume YUY2/MJPG.
verified.note: Both quotes match. Whether a DS app can then stream from such a source, beyond enumerating it, is not stated.

verified.claim: DS-filter virtual cameras are invisible to MF; Chromium keeps a DS enumeration pass to pick them up.
verified.corrected_claim: Chromium's AugmentDevicesListWithDirectShowOnlyDevices() carries this comment: 'DirectShow virtual cameras are not supported by MediaFoundation. To overcome this, based on device name and model, we append missing DirectShow device descriptor to full devices list.' It also swaps in DS descriptors when only DS reports supported formats.
verified.note: The report's quote was slightly paraphrased; the substance matches.

verified.claim: Chromium made MF the default Windows capture backend in Jan 2019 after a 100% stable rollout since Oct 2018; MF is still enabled by default; DS remains as a fallback.
verified.corrected_claim: Chromium commit c4f58b38 (Christian Fremerey, 2019-01-11) enabled MediaFoundationVideoCapture by default, noting it 'has been enabled per finch config at 100% on stable since October.' Current media_switches.cc has BASE_FEATURE(kMediaFoundationVideoCapture, base::FEATURE_ENABLED_BY_DEFAULT). Chromium keeps DirectShow for blocked devices, DS-only devices and devices for which MF reports no formats.
verified.note: Verified through the GitHub mirror and the raw source. I did not verify the 'Windows 8+' scope.

verified.claim: Chromium still forces specific USB webcams onto DS because MF misbehaves with them, the list keeps growing, and it falls back to DS when MF reports no formats.
verified.corrected_claim: Chromium's kModelIdsBlockedForMediaFoundation ('Use this list only for USB webcams') sends listed VID:PIDs to DirectShow. Many entries are capture cards or bridge chips (Empia 2860/2820, Elgato HD60 Pro, Elgato Cam Link 4K, Sensoray 2253, Hauppauge USB-Live2) or laptop-integrated cameras (Dell E5440/E7440, Lenovo ThinkPad, HP EliteBook 840 G1, HP HD Camera, Acer, the Windows Hello RGB/IR camera). Only a few are standalone webcams: TOSHIBA Web Camera - HD (crbug 420284824) and Microsoft LifeCam Studio 045e:0772 (crbug 535635412). The code does not state the failure modes. A separate list blocks D3D11 on MF for 05a3:9331 and 04f2:b6bf (E_MF_SAMPLEALLOCATOREMPTY), and VMware Virtual Webcam is blocked because it hangs. Commit 37726611 (2018-07-17) added a DS fallback when MF offers no video format (Pinnacle Dazzle).
verified.note: The listed entries are real, but the report left out about 12 entries that show the list is mostly capture cards and integrated laptop cameras. 'Keeps growing' rests only on the high crbug numbers of the newest entries; the commit history was not fetched (HTTP 429). The crbug pages require sign-in, so the failure modes are unknown. None of the entries is a skellycam camera.

verified.claim: Chromium's DS path uses only IMediaSample start time (stream-relative, wall-clock fallback); its MF path reads the device capture QPC time (MFSampleExtension_DeviceReferenceSystemTime).
verified.corrected_claim: Chromium's DS sink takes the timestamp from IMediaSample::GetTime start_time. When the timestamp is missing, the device falls back to TimeTicks::Now() minus the first reference time. Chromium's MF path also takes its main timestamp from IMFSample::GetSampleTime. It reads MFSampleExtension_DeviceReferenceSystemTime (falling back to MFGetSystemTime()) only to compute capture_begin_time. That value is forwarded only when the kMediaFoundationVideoCaptureForwardSampleTimestamps feature is enabled, and that feature is FEATURE_DISABLED_BY_DEFAULT.
verified.note: By default, Chromium's MF path does not deliver the device QPC capture time. Both paths use a sample time, so the claimed MF timestamp advantage in Chromium is overstated.

verified.claim: Microsoft documents that DS preview-pin frames carry no timestamps; for single-pin cameras the Smart Tee strips timestamps from preview and delivers preview only when it does not hurt capture.
verified.corrected_claim: Time Stamps doc: in video capture, 'Every sample is time stamped with a start time equal to the stream time when it was captured', except that 'Video frames from a preview pin (as opposed to a capture pin) are not time stamped.' Smart Tee doc: it is used 'when a video capture filter does not provide separate pins for capture and preview', 'delivers preview data only if doing so does not hurt capture performance', and 'removes the time stamps from the preview stream'. The capture pin (Smart Tee output 0) keeps its timestamps.
verified.note: The quotes are exact. This is a consequence of how a DS graph is built (use the capture pin), not a limit of DS itself, so it favours neither stack.

verified.claim: OpenCV CAP_DSHOW discards DS timestamps: PREVIEW-pin graph, NULL sync source, SampleTime ignored, RGB24 forced (decoder inserted); so CAP_DSHOW timing problems are OpenCV's design.
verified.corrected_claim: OpenCV 4.x cap_dshow.cpp uses the preview pin when one exists (otherwise the Smart Tee preview), calls RenderStream(&PIN_CATEGORY_PREVIEW, ...), calls pMediaFilter->SetSyncSource(NULL), and declares SampleCB(double, IMediaSample*) with the time argument unnamed. The grabber is set to MEDIASUBTYPE_RGB24 unless the source is a single-byte format, Y16 or NV12, so MJPG sources get a decoder inserted. CAP_DSHOW's lack of timestamps is a property of OpenCV's graph, not of DirectShow.
verified.note: All four code facts reproduce. RGB24 is not forced for every format.

verified.claim: FFmpeg dshow historically ignored device video timestamps as unreliable; since 2021-12-24 (FFmpeg 5.0+) it uses device timestamps by default with workarounds for missing/garbage times.
verified.corrected_claim: Commit 7dc33aad (authored 2021-12-21, committed 2021-12-24, first in n5.0) added use_video_device_timestamps, default 1, because 'the majority of video devices out there probably provide fine timestamps'. dshow_pin.c still falls back to the graph clock when the sample time is not set or is 0, and drops samples with a PTS above 4e17. On this machine, however, the device sample times dshow returns for the C922 and C930e are constant to 100 ns (for example exactly 333333). That makes them synthesized or regularized values, not per-frame measurements.
verified.note: The facts are confirmed. Local evidence shows 'device timestamps' on DS are nominal for these cameras, so 'favours MF' should rest on MF's UVC metadata, not on this commit.

verified.claim: Local tests: PyAV dshow pts are nominal 33.333 ms steps drifting 1.42 s from arrival in 10 s on the generic camera; MF llTimestamp matched the device timestamp on 100% of frames and carried the UVC payload header on the C922/C930e.
verified.corrected_claim: mjpeg_passthrough_summary.md:88 says exactly this. Related local findings qualify it. MF sample times and all host arrival times are quantized in about 16 ms steps (±8 ms at best), and accurate timing needs the UVC PTS/SCR carried in MF's 32-byte payload-header metadata. That metadata appeared only after a one-time admin registry value was set (MetadataBufferSizeInKB0).
verified.note: The quote is accurate. MF's real advantage is access to the UVC header, not llTimestamp alone, because llTimestamp is also on the 16 ms grid.

verified.claim: PyAV/FFmpeg dshow vcodec=mjpeg is a working native JPEG path, byte-identical headers to MF, full rate, ~1-2% CPU; DS not worse than MF on byte delivery.
verified.corrected_claim: For the C922, C930e and 4C4A:4A55, PyAV dshow with vcodec=mjpeg delivered 100% valid JPEG at 30.04/30.04/25.74 fps (720p), using 0.9-1.6% of one core, with DQT/SOF/DHT header hashes matching MF (11 of 14 generic headers matched the single MF cell). PyAV did not deliver MJPEG for the Razer Kiyo Pro (rawvideo YUY2 at 720p and 1080p), while SDL3 over MF did deliver MJPEG for the Kiyo.
verified.note: Confirmed for the three test cameras. The Kiyo case, which the report omitted, is a counterexample where the dshow path lost MJPEG and an MF path kept it.

verified.claim: FFmpeg/PyAV has no MF camera input; dshow is its only modern Windows camera demuxer, so the pure-Python no-compile route to native JPEG on Windows is DS.
verified.corrected_claim: The ffmpeg-devices input list has dshow, gdigrab and vfwcap for Windows and no Media Foundation input, so the PyAV route is DirectShow. It is not the only no-compile Python route, though. GStreamer mfvideosrc (pip gstreamer-bundle) and SDL3's MF camera API both delivered native JPEG bytes on this machine without compiling anything.
verified.note: The FFmpeg fact is confirmed. The 'therefore DS' conclusion is contradicted by the repo's own prior-art results.

verified.claim: FFmpeg dshow drops frames itself when rtbufsize fills, with a probabilistic drop score; slow consumers silently lose frames logged only as errors.
verified.corrected_claim: dshow.c shall_we_drop() drops frames when the real-time buffer is near full, using dropscore {62,75,87,100}, and logs 'real-time buffer ... too full or near too full ... frame dropped!'. A consumer that falls behind loses frames, and the only signal is that log line.
verified.note: This is a wrapper (FFmpeg) behaviour, not a DirectShow one. A custom DS graph or an MF reader also drops frames if the consumer lags.

verified.claim: Multi-camera USB bandwidth failures look the same on DS and MF locally; public DS reports show the same error class.
verified.corrected_claim: Locally, a second MJPEG camera on a shared USB 2.0 hub failed on both stacks (MF 0x800718CF, DirectShow OSError 5). In OBS forum thread 124531 (2020-06-14), a user running five cameras, some through a hub, got 'Run failed (0x800705AA): Insufficient system resources'. The problem 'seemed better' after they stopped using the hub, and another member advised against hubs and for per-port controller cards.
verified.note: The OBS fix was tentative ('seemed better'), not a confirmed resolution. The local run also noted that MF twice briefly could not find the generic camera after such a refusal.

verified.claim: OpenCV DS format negotiation is order-fragile: fourcc-first gave YUY2 ~10 fps, size-first gave MJPG 30 fps, neither returned JPEG.
verified.corrected_claim: With OpenCV 4.12 CAP_DSHOW, setting FOURCC before size reproduced YUY2 at 9.99 fps, and setting size first gave MJPG at 30 fps. Both returned decoded BGR, never JPEG bytes.
verified.note: This is an OpenCV wrapper behaviour, not evidence about DirectShow itself, so 'favours MF' is overstated.

verified.claim: DS apps were not insulated from Frame Server in Win10 1607; the MJPEG/H.264 removal broke DS apps like Skype and Kinovea.
verified.corrected_claim: The Kinovea admin wrote on 2016-08-23 that 'a recent auto-update of Windows 10 is breaking MJPEG streams for applications based on DirectShow'. Microsoft 'moved the decoding stage upstream in the pipeline and removed access to the compressed stream', breaking 'many high profile applications like Skype', with a fix expected via auto-update in September. Thurrott (2016-08-19) reported that the Anniversary Update allowed only YUY2 from USB webcams. The workaround was EnableFrameServerMode=0 under HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows Media Foundation\Platform.
verified.note: Confirmed. This was a 2016 regression that Microsoft then fixed. It shows that DS routing through Frame Server has changed between Windows versions, which also undercuts any assumption that DS is permanently isolated from Frame Server changes.

verified.claim: Windows 11 Settings 'Video rotation' strips MJPEG/H.264 and may break legacy apps; Settings defaults are applied whenever an app starts the camera.
verified.corrected_claim: For external cameras, any Video rotation other than 'No rotation' makes Windows remove all compressed types, such as MJPEG and H.264, and output only uncompressed types, and 'Legacy applications and cameras that depend on compressed data types ... might not function correctly'. Settings default values are applied when an app opens and starts the camera, unless the app wrote that control after opening and before starting the stream.
verified.note: The quotes are exact. The default is No rotation. The doc does not say whether non-bridged DS apps are affected, so for DS this risk is undocumented.

verified.claim: Windows Studio Effects only applies to NPU devices and the integrated front-facing camera, irrelevant to external USB webcams.
verified.corrected_claim: Studio Effects needs Windows 11 22H2 (build 22623.885+), a supported NPU, and the OEM's opt-in driver. It 'currently supports front-facing camera'. Once enabled, it applies to any app using that camera.
verified.note: Confirmed. Intel's OBS PR #10471 likewise says its NPU features work only on OEM-integrated webcams.

verified.claim: New Windows camera AI features reach OBS only via an MF source; Intel wrote a separate MF source (PR still open); a 2025 PR cited cameras DS cannot open.
verified.corrected_claim: Intel's OBS PR #10471 (2024-04-02, still open) adds an MF-based 'Video Capture Device 2' for Intel NPU effects. It states the features work only on OEM-integrated webcams and that external USB support was not yet available. PR #12816 (2025-11-13) was closed within an hour after a maintainer pointed to #10471. Its 'Some cameras do not open by dshow' is unsupported by any device detail.
verified.note: The PR facts are accurate. The report left out that the AI features exclude external USB cameras, and the DS-failure line is an unsupported assertion. This is irrelevant to skellycam's cameras.

verified.claim: On Windows on ARM, DS filters are per-architecture registrations; OBS's DS virtual camera was invisible to native ARM64 apps until the ARM64 DLL was registered; DS stacks need separate x64/ARM64 builds while MF/Frame Server is brokered by the OS.
verified.corrected_claim: In an OBS forum thread (Jan 2025 to Jan 2026), users on ARM64 and Snapdragon reported that the OBS virtual camera did not show up in other apps. One user (2026-01-12) reported an unofficial fix: copy and regsvr32 obs-virtualcam-module-arm64.dll. After that the ARM64 Zoom build worked, and Teams worked under x64 emulation. One earlier poster in the thread was on an AMD Surface.
verified.note: This is one user's workaround for a virtual-camera filter. The general claim about DS versus MF architecture is inference, and skellycam does not ship a DS filter, so it has little relevance.

verified.claim: An old OpenCV bug reports MJPG artifacts via CAP_DSHOW on C920 and ELP at non-default resolutions.
verified.corrected_claim: OpenCV issue #11324 (2018-04-16, still open; OpenCV 3.2, Windows 10) reports a black last row and other artifacts when MJPG was set through CAP_DSHOW at 1280x720 on a C920 and an ELP camera. A 2019 commenter attributed the problem to the ELP camera.
verified.note: This is an OpenCV 3.2 wrapper report with no root cause, not evidence against DirectShow MJPEG. 'Favours MF' is not supported.

verified.claim: The Microsoft MJPEG Decompressor handles only FOURCC 'MJPG' and has no documented threading/performance characteristics.
verified.corrected_claim: The MJPEG Decompressor (quartz.dll, MERIT_NORMAL) 'is compatible with motion JPEG video that uses the FOURCC code MJPG. It cannot decode other varieties of motion JPEG.' The page documents no performance or threading behaviour.
verified.note: Confirmed. It is irrelevant to a passthrough design that never decodes inside DS.

verified.claim: DirectShow still ships and is serviced in current Windows 11 (qcap.dll 10.0.26100.8875).
verified.corrected_claim: On this Windows 11 machine (10.0.26300), qcap.dll ('DirectShow Runtime.') has product version 10.0.26100.8875, and mfksproxy.dll is 10.0.26100.9549. Both carry recent servicing build numbers.
verified.note: Confirmed. A servicing build number shows the binary is rebuilt, not that DS gets new features.

verified.claim: DMFTs are MF components; Microsoft recommends NV12/YUY2 not MJPEG outputs, so vendor-DMFT cameras may hide MJPEG from MF apps; none of the skellycam cameras registers CameraDeviceMftClsid.
verified.corrected_claim: The Device MFT Design Guide recommends DMFT output in NV12, then YUY2, and says 'MJPEG and RGB media types aren't recommended.' It also says 'On 64-bit systems that don't make use of Frame Server, both 32-bit and 64-bit DMFTs must be registered.' I re-read the interface Device Parameters for the C922, C930e and 4C4A:4A55 read-only: there is no CameraDeviceMftClsid, CameraDeviceMftCLSIDChain or EnablePlatformDmft.
verified.note: Confirmed. The Platform DMFT chain key was not checked in the original report; it is also absent. DMFTs live in the MF pipeline, so DS apps that bypass it do not get DMFT processing.

missed: MF-side flakiness, local: OpenCV CAP_MSMF takes 39-41 s to open each Logitech camera (3.4-3.7 s for the generic) on the test machine. This is the likely 'MF is flaky' folklore source, and it is an OpenCV MSMF wrapper problem (hardware-transform setup). Forum reports show the same pattern: a C910 took minutes under MSMF but opened at once under DSHOW, and OPENCV_VIDEOIO_MSMF_ENABLE_HW_TRANSFORMS=0 is the usual fix. Sources: research/usb_cameras/mjpeg/RESULTS.md:129; research/REPORT.md:40; https://forum.opencv.org/t/using-opencv4-7-0-cap-open-0-to-open-the-camera-is-slow/13954 ; https://forum.opencv.org/t/the-msmf-backend-is-slow-to-acquire-the-initial-frame/24121
MF-side flakiness, local: twice, MF briefly could not find the generic camera right after a USB bandwidth refusal (research/usb_cameras/docs/mjpeg_passthrough_summary.md, camera-health section).

Frame Server reliability reports: (a) Microsoft Q&A, 2023-10-30, Windows 11 22H2 with a Logitech C920. The Frame Server Monitor crashed several times a minute (KERNELBASE C++ exception), and the thread was locked unresolved: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/4102987/windows-camera-frame-server-monitor-continually-cr . (b) Microsoft Q&A, 2024-07-16, Windows 11. IMFActivate::ActivateObject occasionally froze for 5-10 minutes after cameras were plugged in often, leaving every camera unusable until the wait ended or the PC rebooted; no fix was given: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/1819830/why-does-the-interface-get-stuck-for-5-10-minutes . Both are relevant to one process per camera with hot-plugging, and both are MF/Frame Server failure modes that a non-bridged DS path might avoid.

Local timing evidence the report left out: the DirectShow device sample times returned through PyAV/FFmpeg are constant to 100 ns (333333 on the C922), so they are synthesized, not measured. MF IMFSample times (seen through SDL3) and all host arrival times fall on an approximately 16 ms grid, which limits them to about ±8 ms. Only the UVC PTS/SCR, which reached MF after a one-time admin registry value was set, gave about 0.4-1.8 ms error. MF's timing advantage therefore comes from UVC metadata access, not from MF sample timestamps. Sources: research/usb_cameras/prior_art/SURVEY.md:50,56-69; research/usb_cameras/docs/usb_camera_report.md:40-58; research/REPORT.md:29.

Native-JPEG MF paths that need no compiling, measured locally: GStreamer 1.28 mfvideosrc (pip gstreamer-bundle) and SDL3 3.4.18's MF camera API both delivered 100% valid native JPEG. SDL3 also did so on the Kiyo Pro, where PyAV dshow fell back to YUY2 rawvideo (research/usb_cameras/prior_art/SURVEY.md:48-53).

The UVC Camera Implementation Guide says devices that publish UVC-CPV2FaceAuth do not need EnableDshowRedirection to be bridged; it is still required for older Windows or for MJPEG decoding in Frame Server. So the bridge opt-in is not the only route (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/stream/uvc-camera-implementation-guide).

On this machine, HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\OEM\DshowBridge\1 (and the WOW6432Node copy) has Application=Launcher_Main.exe, Productname=Logitech Camera Software, and mfksproxy.dll references the 'Application' and 'ProductName' values. DS-to-MF bridging therefore appears to also be controlled per application, a mechanism that is undocumented.

The same Microsoft maintainer comment that calls DS legacy also says 'Some apps do still support DShow sources in some capacity such as Teams, Skype, Zoom', and that DS-filter virtual cameras 'can incur issues if modified from 1 client while concurrently used from another' (https://github.com/microsoft/Windows-Camera/issues/72, 2024-11-19).

Chromium also blocks MF+D3D11 for two USB webcams (05a3:9331, 04f2:b6bf) because 'MFCaptureEngine fails with E_MF_SAMPLEALLOCATOREMPTY', and blocks 'VMware Virtual Webcam' because it hangs under MF. Separately, the MF path's device-QPC capture_begin_time forwarding (kMediaFoundationVideoCaptureForwardSampleTimestamps) is disabled by default (video_capture_device_factory_win.cc l.172-184; video_capture_device_mf_win.cc l.57).

Relevant to the user's relayed question about the Windows timer: this verification step did not research it, but the evidence bears on it. The ~16 ms arrival/sample-time grid measured locally matches the default Windows timer tick of 15.625 ms. Microsoft's timeBeginPeriod doc says that before Windows 10 2004 the call set a global timer resolution. From 2004 on it affects only the calling process ('Windows does not guarantee a higher resolution than the default system resolution' for other processes). From Windows 11, a window-owning process that is fully occluded, minimized or invisible may lose the higher resolution (see SetProcessInformation, PROCESS_POWER_THROTTLING_IGNORE_TIMER_RESOLUTION). The old practice of running a helper program that raises the resolution for every process therefore no longer works on current Windows; each capture process must request it itself (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/timeapi/nf-timeapi-timebeginperiod, updated 2024-02-22). Whether the 16 ms camera grid is caused by the timer tick or by USB/usbvideo.sys completion timing has not been tested (SURVEY.md lists the latter as an unverified hypothesis).

verified.claim: The 15.6 ms DateTime.UtcNow / C# timer-resolution story is designed behavior, not a bug: DateTime.UtcNow wraps GetSystemTimeAsFileTime, which advances only on the clock interrupt; anything raising global timer resolution made it advance every 1 ms.
verified.corrected_claim: In 2012 Osenkov saw DateTime.UtcNow change 3 times in 50 ms on one machine and 50 times on another. He first blamed the OS version, then retracted that. A commenter explained that DateTime.UtcNow calls GetSystemTimeAsFileTime: precision is 100 ns, but accuracy follows the timer interval (15.6 ms or 1 ms). The commenter's ClockRes output showed a Win7 SP1 machine at 1 ms. Commenters named multimedia timers as a common cause of the higher rate and powercfg /energy as a way to find which program is responsible. A later comment links Lucas Hale's tool 'to modify the system timer'. The source never uses the word 'bug'; calling it designed behavior is an inference, though a well-supported one.
verified.note: The quotes and numbers match. Scope: Win7 / Server 2008 R2 and .NET Framework only. Stale for modern .NET: the current dotnet/runtime DateTime.Windows.cs uses GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime when it exists and agrees with GetSystemTimeAsFileTime to within 100 ms (see missed).

verified.claim: Default tick 15.625 ms (64 Hz) is the documented coarse clock; GetTickCount64 and GetSystemTimeAsFileTime are documented as 10-16 ms resolution APIs.
verified.corrected_claim: Microsoft's timestamps page has a table row 'PC RTC | 64 Hz | 15.625 milliseconds'. It also says: 'If resolution of 10 to 16 milliseconds is sufficient, you can use GetTickCount64, QueryInterruptTime, QueryUnbiasedInterruptTime...', and 'For UTC-synchronized time stamps, use GetSystemTimeAsFileTime'.
verified.note: Minor scope point: the 64 Hz row is labeled 'PC RTC' in a table of nominal clock sources. The page does not say in so many words that the scheduler interrupt defaults to 15.625 ms. The 10-16 ms sentence also lists QueryInterruptTime and QueryUnbiasedInterruptTime.

verified.claim: Windows 10 2004 changed timeBeginPeriod so it no longer sets global resolution for every process; one process can no longer reliably fix timer behavior for others.
verified.corrected_claim: The timeBeginPeriod doc says: 'Starting with Windows 10, version 2004, this function no longer affects global timer resolution... For processes which have not called this function, Windows does not guarantee a higher resolution than the default system resolution.' Before 2004 it was a global setting. What changed is the guarantee to other processes. In practice the interrupt rate is still global (see claims 5 and 7).
verified.note: The quote is verbatim.

verified.claim: Windows 11: an occluded/minimized/invisible window-owning process may have its timer-resolution request ignored; a process can opt in via SetProcessInformation(ProcessPowerThrottling, IGNORE_TIMER_RESOLUTION).
verified.corrected_claim: timeBeginPeriod doc: 'Starting with Windows 11, if a window-owning process becomes fully occluded, minimized, or otherwise invisible or inaudible to the end user, Windows does not guarantee a higher resolution than the default system resolution.' SetProcessInformation doc: with PROCESS_POWER_THROTTLING_IGNORE_TIMER_RESOLUTION 'any current timer resolution requests made by the process will be ignored'. It also says that by default in Windows 11 'Windows may automatically ignore the timer resolution request' of such a process.
verified.note: The wording is 'may' and 'does not guarantee', not 'will'. The rule applies only to window-owning processes, so windowless console or background camera processes are not clearly covered.

verified.claim: Even after 2004, timeBeginPeriod still raises the hardware timer interrupt rate globally; only guarantees changed. Change was undocumented until 2021.
verified.corrected_claim: Bruce Dawson (2020, updated 2021): 'timeBeginPeriod still sets the global timer interrupt interval, on all versions of Window.' He said the docs were not updated at first, and a 2021 update notes that the change 'is acknowledged now in the timeBeginPeriod documentation'. Dawson does not discuss GetSystemTimeAsFileTime. The idea that 'any value tied to the interrupt' is affected is an extrapolation, but the local measurement supports it for GetSystemTimeAsFileTime.
verified.strength: expert blog (Chrome/Windows performance engineer), not a Microsoft statement

Dawson replied: 'I wouldn't recommend setting that (except for test purposes)... software definitely shouldn't set it on user machines.' In the default run, time.time_ns had a median step of 500.1 us (max 1278.9) and GetSystemTimeAsFileTime 500.1 us (max 1048.0). After timeBeginPeriod(1): 500.1 / 500.0 us. verified.claim: Precise APIs don't depend on the tick: GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime steps ~0.4 us (call cost); QPF = 10 MHz.

verified.claim: On Python 3.12, time.monotonic uses GetTickCount64 and steps 16 ms even with system timer at 0.5 ms; get_clock_info('time') reports 0.015625 though observed step was 0.5 ms.

The resolution reported for time() is the nominal 15.625 ms increment, not the 0.5 ms update rate actually observed.

verified.claim: Real Windows timer bugs affected QPC on old hardware/Windows (pre-Vista TSC issues, KB274323 'leap forward'); current Windows checks TSC at boot and falls back to HPET/PM timer, so apps needn't work around it.
verified.corrected_claim: Microsoft's timestamps doc says that on XP/2000, 'Systems with flawed firmware... might not provide the same QPC reading on different cores'. It says Windows checks TSC suitability at initialization and picks HPET or the ACPI PM timer when the TSC is unsuitable. Its FAQ says 'You don't need to perform such checks' and that QPC is monotonic. KB274323 ('Performance counter value may unexpectedly leap forward') is a chipset-era QPC issue, known here only from third-party projects (pjproject, PortAudio, AutoIt) that added workarounds. Mozilla bug 836869 is about making Firefox's own QPC leap-detection heuristic smarter. Its platform field is Windows 7, and the '64-bit Windows XP' line is a quoted blog sentence. It was fixed in mozilla23.
verified.note: The cited Mozilla page does not mention KB274323 and does not support the Microsoft-doc statements; those come from the MS page. verified.claim: skellycam per-frame timestamps use time.perf_counter_ns() (QPC), so unaffected by tick rate; since Python 3.10 perf_counter is the same clock in all processes on Windows.
verified.corrected_claim: opencv_get_frame.py:53-72 records the grab and retrieve timestamps with time.perf_counter_ns(), and opencv_camera_loop.py uses it at lines 36, 80, 95, 97, 117, 145 and 159. Python docs: perf_counter 'Changed in version 3.10: On Windows, the clock is now the same for all processes.' On 3.12 perf_counter is QueryPerformanceCounter (resolution 1e-07), so these timestamps do not depend on the system tick rate.
verified.note: These timestamps are taken in user space around cap.grab(), not at sensor exposure. Tick rate is irrelevant to them, but they still carry driver and scheduling latency.

verified.claim: TimebaseMapping anchors UTC with time.time_ns() (GetSystemTimeAsFileTime on 3.12), giving a constant offset error up to one tick (~0.5 ms here, ~15.6 ms at default); each mapping instance gets a different offset; fix via GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime or Python 3.13+.
verified.corrected_claim: timebase_mapping.py:22-23 takes utc_time_ns from time.time_ns and perf_counter_ns from time.perf_counter_ns as two separate default_factory calls. On CPython 3.11/3.12 on Windows, time.time_ns lags true UTC by between 0 and one interrupt period (0.5 ms on this machine now, up to 15.625 ms at the default tick). So converted UTC timestamps carry a constant bias of up to one tick per mapping, about half a tick on average, in the 'too early' direction. Relative frame timing is unaffected. Within a camera group a single mapping is shared: process_and_save_recording_timestamps.py:59-64 checks that every frame's mapping is identical. So cameras in one recording share the same offset. audio_recorder.py:169 creates its own TimebaseMapping(), so audio and video UTC anchors can differ by up to one tick. Python 3.13+ or a ctypes call to GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime removes the tick quantization.
verified.note: 'Each mapping instance gets a different offset' is true, but it overstates the practical effect: frames in one recording share a single mapping. The mapping is also a one-shot anchor, so NTP slewing of system time and oscillator drift (claim 17) accumulate after it is taken. Those errors are separate from the tick quantization.

verified.claim: time.sleep no longer depends on timeBeginPeriod on Win10+ with Python 3.11+ (high-resolution waitable timer); locally sleep(0.001) median ~1.5 ms.
verified.corrected_claim: Python docs: 'On Windows 10 and newer the implementation uses a high-resolution timer which provides resolution of 100 nanoseconds'; 'Changed in version 3.11: ... On Windows, a waitable timer is now used.' In the verifier's re-run, time.sleep(0.001) had a median of 1.506 ms (max 1.524) by default and 1.506 ms (max 1.612) after timeBeginPeriod(1).
verified.note: The local test cannot show independence from timeBeginPeriod, because the global rate was already 0.5 ms. The roughly 0.5 ms overshoot means actual sleep granularity on this machine is nowhere near the documented '100 ns resolution'.

verified.claim: For long recordings oscillator frequency error (30-50 ppm, several seconds/day) matters more than resolution unless re-anchored to UTC.
verified.corrected_claim: Microsoft's doc: PC crystals are 'typically manufactured with a frequency tolerance of ± 30 to 50 parts per million, and rarely... as much as 500 ppm'; '±50 ppm yields a maximum error of ± 4.3 seconds after 24 hours'. The same page says recent Windows versions, especially Windows 8, use multiple hardware timers at boot to detect the frequency offset and compensate for it as far as possible. So the uncompensated 30-50 ppm figure is a worst-case bound, not the expected residual error.
verified.note: The report left out the boot-time calibration sentence, which lowers the expected drift. For a few cameras on one PC all reading the same QPC, drift does not affect relative sync between cameras. It matters only when comparing with UTC or with other machines.

missed: Modern .NET no longer has the coarse DateTime.UtcNow behavior at the center of the 'run some C# code' story. dotnet/runtime src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/DateTime.Windows.cs uses GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime when it exists and agrees with GetSystemTimeAsFileTime to within 100 ms. Its own comment warns that 'on misconfigured systems, it's possible for the "precise" time to be inaccurate'. Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dotnet/runtime/main/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/DateTime.Windows.cs (read 2026-10-28). The proposal was dotnet/coreclr #5883 (2016). The exact .NET release that shipped the switch was not confirmed, and .NET Framework 4.x behavior was not checked. On current Windows 11 with current .NET, the C# 15.6 ms symptom is mostly gone unless the code runs on .NET Framework.

No register is involved. The 'C# code to make the timer update' was almost certainly a program calling timeBeginPeriod or NtSetTimerResolution (for example Lucas Hale's TimerResolution, or the 'timer resolution' rules in Process Lasso: https://bitsum.com/apps/process-lasso/docs/rules/timer-resolution/). Process Lasso documents that since Win10 2004 such an adjustment has no effect on processes that do not request a resolution themselves 'unless you have checked Apply globally'. This partly contradicts the local finding that GetSystemTimeAsFileTime still follows another process's rate. Process Lasso is talking about timer and wait expiry, not time-of-day updates, so the two claims are about different things and both can hold.

The 'Windows 11 rule' may matter for skellycam: the docs say requests from occluded or minimized window-owning processes may be ignored. If the program that currently holds 0.5 ms (unidentified; it could be a browser, Razer or LogiTune software, etc.) gets minimized or closed, coarse clocks on this machine fall back to 15.625 ms. So the 0.5 ms observed today is not a stable property of the machine. Source: timeBeginPeriod and SetProcessInformation docs above.

Windows Internals, as quoted by a 2023-03-24 comment on Dawson's post: modern Windows 10 'no longer necessarily run on a periodic tick' (dynamic tick). How often the coarse clock updates can therefore also vary with idle state, not only with resolution requests. Not verified against the book itself. Source: https://randomascii.wordpress.com/2020/10/04/windows-timer-resolution-the-great-rule-change/ (comments).

No evidence found of any current Windows 11 bug in which the system time 'fails to update at regular intervals'. Searches for 22H2, 23H2 or 24H2 timer or GetSystemTimeAsFileTime regressions returned nothing specific. Dawson's comments up to 2025 contain no Windows 11 timing regressions beyond the registry-key anecdote.

The report did not note that Python 3.13 also makes perf_counter the same clock as monotonic ('Changed in version 3.13: Use the same clock as time.monotonic()'). That is harmless for skellycam, because both are QPC on 3.13. https://docs.python.org/3/library/time.html
